source.title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization
source.authors: Sekh Mainul Islam; Pepa Atanasova; Isabelle Augenstein

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent garbling or truncation.
record.tranche_reason: Applies feature probing and crosscoder analysis to personalized MoE LLMs, extending feature-representation analysis to this model type and setting. It does not reproduce the original toy-network method.
record.gate_note: The study tests whether personalization features are decodable and recoverable with crosscoder latents, and compares polysemanticity-related measures between MoE and dense models. It does not test toy-model superposition geometry or capacity competition. Personalization benchmark scores, routing-layer selection criteria, and cited results from other work are not included as rows because they do not directly measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: Trains BatchTopK crosscoders (SAE-type dictionaries) on three MoE LLMs. It reports how interpretable the recovered latents are (autointerp F1) and how much activation variance they explain. These bear on V4 (an SAE recovers sparse interpretable features) and on V5's completeness. The k-sparse probing compares MoE with dense models but gives no readable numbers and does not measure how widely features spread in absolute terms. The patching and expert-routing results concern fine-tune-specific latents and experts, not whether dictionary features are the model's units.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that MoE LLMs personalize competitively using about 20% of parameters and show lower polysemanticity than dense models of similar active size. They also conclude that crosscoders isolate a small set of interpretable personalization latents. They claim these latents suffice to recover personalized behaviour, that mapped experts are necessary, and that features follow distinct routing paths. The record should note that the authors limit the MoE-dense disentanglement comparison to the same model family.
record.recipe_differences: Uses personalization fine-tuning, k-sparse probes, crosscoders, and causal interventions on pretrained MoE LLMs; it does not use the original toy-network setup or measure superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe results vary with k; the paper says the MoE–dense gap remains wide at k=1 for same-family Olmo and Qwen comparisons. Crosscoder interpretation scores rise with activation strength. Selected personalized latents depend on the decoder-norm threshold. Crosscoder reconstruction quality differs by model.

fits_no_version.finding: k-sparse probes on MoE expert neurons decode personalization concepts better than matched dense MLP neurons, with the gap still wide at k=1 (within the OLMo and Qwen families).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse MoE architectures reduce neuron polysemanticity relative to dense models of similar active size.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding the decoder contributions of fine-tune-specific crosscoder latents reduces the KL divergence to the personalized model more than frequency-matched random or shared latents (p<0.001). The absolute reduction looks small (axes top out near 12%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Crosscoder diff latents causally capture part of the behaviour change introduced by fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Latent-to-expert mappings show stability S of 0.81 and distinctiveness D of 0.94 (Qwen3). Steering the mapped experts moves the non-personalized model toward the personalized one.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distinct dictionary features route through distinct MoE experts.

record.problems: The study analyzes personalization features in only three MoE families and one selected layer per model. Dense comparisons differ in pretraining data and recipes. Crosscoder reconstruction is imperfect and selected latents depend on a threshold. Probe labels apply response-level concepts to individual tokens, and selecting the best component may favor MoEs with more candidates. Expert attribution is correlational and depends on sample and selection choices. Explanation evaluation uses an LLM explainer/scorer.
record.rows_left_out: No other directly relevant results were omitted. Expert-mapping stability/distinctiveness and steering results concern expert routing paths, which none of the listed versions specifically names; the paper's own claims about those results are summarized in authors_conclusion. Numerical plotted values that were not given in text are recorded as figure only.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, phase transition or geometry.
Does not test capacity competition. The MoE-vs-dense contrast confounds width and sparsity with pretraining data and recipe.
No alternative cause of polysemanticity is tested.
No quantified spread of features across neurons in dense models; the probe values are figure-only.
Stability across seeds or dictionary sizes and canonicity are not tested. The stability S measured is for latent-to-expert mappings, not for the features themselves.
No test of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Explanation F1 for the lower activation bins (0–95%), plotted only
Numeric KL-reduction percentages with 95% bootstrap CIs for personalized, random and shared latents
ν ratio (β_base/β_ft) comparing MoE and dense personalized latents; Mixtral is higher than Llama-2-13B

record.verdict_notes: The crosscoder is a BatchTopK SAE-type dictionary trained on paired activations, so V4/V5 links are by analogy to SAEs. The rows' V5 'supports' label from patching is dropped: the patching concerns fine-tune-diff latents, not whether features are complete or canonical units, and the recovered KL fraction looks modest. The latent counts (r10–r12) are selection values. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-count-versus-dimension sweep, overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transition is tested.

The study compares polysemanticity-related probe results but does not test whether limited capacity causes feature competition, or whether important features get dedicated dimensions while others share.
No alternative cause of polysemantic neurons is tested.
Tests sparse probing and crosscoder recovery of personalization features in three MoE LLMs, but not a general account of feature spreading across neurons in LLMs.

Tests crosscoder feature interpretability and whether selected latents suffice for a measured personalization-related behavior. It does not establish that SAE/crosscoder features are complete, canonical, or stable units across models, tasks, or training runs.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features or test the geometry of superposed features.
